stories.headline: Source: No discipline for A'ja Wilson over fan confrontation
stories.summary: Aces star A'ja Wilson will not face any further discipline over her confrontation with a fan during Tuesday's Game 2 against the Fever, a source told ESPN.
stories.body:
Las Vegas Aces star A'ja Wilson will not face any further discipline over her confrontation with a fan during Tuesday's Game 2 against the Indiana Fever, a source told ESPN on Thursday.

The ruling means Wilson will be fully available for Thursday's decisive Game 3 in the Aces' first-round series against the Fever.

With just over four minutes left in the fourth quarter, Indiana's Sophie Cunningham was called for a foul on Wilson. As Cunningham protested the foul, a fan seated behind the baseline stood up and pointed at Wilson.

Wilson stepped toward the fan and said, "You don't point at me, you don't point at me." As the fan started to sit back down, Aces players Cheyenne Parker-Tyus, Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young came over to pull away Wilson, as did Las Vegas' Kierstan Bell, who left the bench to do so.

The source noted that Wilson remained in the designated court area during the incident and did not step into the stands. The officials gave Wilson a technical foul but concluded no ejection was needed, and the league followed in ruling that no other penalties would be given.

The fan was escorted out of the arena bowl but was allowed back in and took his seat, with the Fever saying arena security spoke with the fan involved as well as witnesses and allowed him to return because "there was no violation of the Fan Code of Conduct."

In the Aces' postgame news conference, Wilson called the fan's actions "unacceptable" and said she was surprised he was allowed to return to his seat.

"I try to play my game ... but if I am just walking, just got the foul, I'm chilling and I see a man come at me, taking steps toward me and pointing at me, I don't give a damn what you said," she said. "I don't give a damn how you said it, the tone. That is unacceptable. You don't step toward me. You never should sit and point at me. That there is unacceptable."

Wilson said she apologized to her teammates for receiving a technical, "but it's just certain things that I'm not going to allow anymore."

"You don't know me at all," she said. "To come and step toward me and point at me and say anything ... you don't have to like me, you don't have to love me. You can hate me with all your heart. But you don't know me. But I guarantee you will respect me."

A WNBA spokesperson had said after the game that the incident would be reviewed.

Game 3 of the Aces-Fever series is Thursday in Las Vegas, with the winner advancing to face the winner of the Dallas Wings-Golden State Valkyries series.

ESPN's Alexa Philippou and Michael Voepel contributed to this report.

stories.headline: UEFA receives Real Madrid dossier on Barcelona-Negreira case
stories.summary: UEFA has received "a substantial amount of documents" from Real Madrid related to its ongoing inquiry into the Negreira case, European football's governing body said on Thursday.
stories.body:
MADRID -- UEFA has received "a substantial amount of documents" from Real Madrid related to its ongoing inquiry into the Negreira case, European football's governing body said on Thursday.

Payments made by Barcelona to companies linked to José María Enriquez Negreira -- the former vice-president of Spain's Technical Committee of Referees -- over two decades have been subject to a UEFA investigation since 2023, while there is also an ongoing Spanish criminal case.

Barcelona have said the payments, which totaled over €7 million ($7.9m), were made for technical refereeing reports.

- Ronaldo's Portugal walkout is nothing new; he has a long history of rows with coaches

- Source: Mbappé to be available for Clásico

- Raphinha back at Barça, injured in Brazil game

"UEFA can confirm that it has received from Real Madrid CF a substantial amount of documents related to the ongoing investigation into FC Barcelona in the matter involving José María Enríquez Negreira," UEFA confirmed in a statement on Thursday.

"The UEFA Ethics and Disciplinary Inspectors have also received these latest documents which they will assess as part of their ongoing review."

Real Madrid said the dossier included "extensive documentation and evidence regarding events of extraordinary seriousness, which directly affect the integrity of the competition and confidence in the refereeing system."

"Real Madrid C.F. considers it essential that, now that UEFA has this documentation, the investigation proceeds with the utmost urgency until its full conclusion, and that the competent bodies take the appropriate decisions in accordance with the severity of the verified facts," the club said.

"Our club will continue to actively collaborate with UEFA and take all actions within its power to clarify events that it deems incompatible with the principles of integrity, transparency, and fair play that should govern European football."

In May, Madrid president Florentino Pérez said that the club was gathering evidence to submit a dossier to UEFA.

Having previously adopted a conciliatory tone with Barcelona -- saying in 2024 that the two clubs "have to help each other" as they worked together on the proposed European Super League -- Pérez has since been extremely critical of his LaLiga rivals.

"They've stolen seven league [titles] from me," Pérez said in May.

In a statement, Barcelona emphasized that Thursday's development did not equate to "any new proceedings."

"The proceedings were initiated in 2023, with the appointment of two investigators who have since carried out the action they deemed appropriate," Barcelona said. "The Club has always complied with all their requests. These proceedings have not been reopened because they have never been closed.

"The UEFA statement confirms receipt of documentation submitted by Real Madrid and indicates that the investigators will assess it within the framework of the existing investigation. The same text expressly refers, on two occasions, to an investigation and a review that are 'ongoing.' It therefore does not announce the opening, reopening, or reactivation of any proceedings, nor does it contain any assessment of the substance or value of the documentation provided.

"It is up to the investigators to determine what action, if any, they consider appropriate regarding this documentation. As of today, they have not made any new requests to FC Barcelona nor have they forwarded Real Madrid's complaint to the Club. Should they do so, the Club will respond accordingly, as it has done up to now.

"In accordance with the applicable legislation governing this matter, these proceedings are subject to the outcome of the criminal case currently being heard in Spain and will continue to be so."

stories.headline: Downing Street clarifies Andy Burnham's remarks on Man City case
stories.summary: A spokesperson for Andy Burnham has insisted the guilty verdict against Manchester City is "serious" after remarks the Prime Minister made about the case on Wednesday raised eyebrows.
stories.body:
A spokesperson for Andy Burnham has insisted the guilty verdict against Manchester City is "serious" after remarks the Prime Minister made about the case on Wednesday raised eyebrows.

Burnham told the BBC on Wednesday he would be "really concerned" if City's Abu Dhabi owners sold the club in the wake of City being found to have breached the Premier League's financial rules by an independent commission, crediting them with being "a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester."

Burnham also appeared to draw parallels between City's guilty verdict and the handling of a disciplinary case against Everton, the club he supports.

He said he still held the view very firmly that the Toffees were "not fairly treated" and added: "I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and with hindsight I think more people would say that wasn't fair, the way that was handled.

"So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming Prime Minister."

Burnham's comments have drawn criticism on social media and shadow sports minister Louie French called for the Government to "keep politics out of football," with the case set to proceed to an appeal board and a sanctions hearing.

A No. 10 Downing Street spokesman said on Thursday: "As the Prime Minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules.

"He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

- Klopp not preparing for more titles after verdict against Man City

- Man City owners must sell due to 'shame of their guilt' - Jamie Carragher

Meanwhile, a parliamentary select committee wants answers from the permanent secretary of Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) regarding any tax implications of the City case.

The chair of the Treasury Committee, Dame Meg Hillier, has written to JP Marks asking whether he is aware of the commission's findings, in particular what it said about the use of "sham" arrangements to conceal liabilities to staff.

Hillier also asked Marks whether he had asked for an unredacted copy of the decision published on Tuesday.

"While I acknowledge that taxpayer confidentiality may inhibit what you can disclose, I would welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in the case," Hillier wrote.

City are expected to lodge an appeal against the guilty verdict before Friday's deadline, having claimed the commission's decision contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

stories.headline: 2027 NFL draft rankings: Jordan Reid's top 50 prospects, scouting reports
stories.summary: Jordan Reid unveils his debut rankings for the 2027 NFL draft class with 50 players -- including six quarterbacks and an elite wide receiver prospect.
stories.body:
With the calendar turning to October, it's time to start stacking the top prospects in the 2027 NFL draft class, which begins on April 29 in Washington, D.C. I've been watching and evaluating these players for a couple of years in some instances, and these rankings are a compilation of my scouting (both on film and in person) and conversations I've been having with scouts and evaluators around the NFL.

We're going to start these rankings with 50 players, with scouting reports on the top 25, but this list will expand as the draft gets closer and closer. And these rankings will evolve -- some players will shoot up boards, others will fall and still more will ultimately return to school for another year. But this is how I currently see things in the 2027 class.

Let's get to it, starting with arguably the best wide receiver prospect of the past 15-20 years. Underclassmen are marked with an asterisk, and the top names at every position are listed at the bottom.

Jump to:

Rankings by position

1. Jeremiah Smith, WR, Ohio State*
Height: 6-4 | Weight: 222

Smith could have All-Pro potential early in his NFL career as a true No. 1 receiver. He immediately changes the offensive outlook for the team that adds him. He is sure-handed and can glide past defenders with ease. And he's equally as capable of winning with strength at the catch point. Smith's change of direction in routes needs to become sharper, as he can take too many choppy steps when working back toward passers. But he is tough to stop when allowed to attack defenses vertically.

Stats through Sept. 30: 33 receptions for 617 receiving yards (18.7 per catch) and seven touchdowns

2. Leonard Moore, CB, Notre Dame*
Height: 6-2 | Weight: 197

With excellent length, speed and technique, Moore is the prototypical cornerback prospect. His length and physicality allow him to excel when getting hands on receivers in press man coverage. He also has the awareness to identify and defend route concepts in zone coverage. Moore has the ball skills to match receivers, routinely tracking and attacking the ball out of the air. But he needs to improve his discipline and hand timing at the top of routes.

Stats through Sept. 30: Seven tackles, two passes defensed, 0% completion percentage allowed

3. Colin Simmons, Edge, Texas*
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 246

Simmons is an energetic and high-effort pass rusher, with a quick first step to explode past blockers. He has a nifty combination of hesitation moves and shoulder fakes. But he still needs to develop consistent counter moves, as he can get stuck if his initial move isn't effective. Simmons is a powerful run defender, using a strong base and powerful hands to keep his frame clean when setting the edge.

Stats through Sept. 30: 13 tackles, 7.5 sacks, nine tackles for loss, one forced fumble, one fumble recovery

4. Will Echoles, DT, Ole Miss*
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 315

An explosive 3-technique, Echoles is one of the most versatile and well-conditioned interior defenders in the country. He has energetic hands that help him accelerate past blockers, and reliable lower body strength helps him be a malleable run defender. Echoles still needs to make major improvements in his counter moves, as he can get stuck on blockers when his power and initial moves are matched. Plus, he can get caught not being firm on contact and get moved off his spot.

Stats through Sept. 30: 12 tackles, 0.5 sacks, three tackles for loss, one pass defensed

5. Dylan Stewart, Edge, South Carolina*
Height: 6-5 | Weight: 250

With a slender frame, Stewart has rare burst and closing speed as a pass rusher. That allows him to wreak havoc on twists and stunts, though the tools have yet to lead to high-end production at the college level. And he might not have many chances to add to his tape, as he's currently suspended from the team. Stewart must also become more consistent with using his length and shedding against the run.

Stats through Sept. 30: One tackle, one tackle for loss

6. Jordan Seaton, OT, LSU*
Height: 6-5 | Weight: 307

Seaton combines a good blend of awareness, quick hands and lower-body suddenness to be a high-level pass protector. He's also an easy mover in space, which allows him to excel as a puller or on screen plays. Seaton can be trusted on an island, but his biggest area of improvement must come as a run blocker. His hands and feet are inconsistent when driving on blocks to the second level.

Stats through Sept. 30: 264 snaps, 0% pressure rate allowed, 0.7% blown run block rate

7. Yhonzae Pierre, Edge, Alabama
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 251

Pierre is an aggressive defender whose pursuit energy has very little drop-off throughout games. He is equally as effective from a stand-up outside linebacker position or with his hand in the ground. Pierre is a true havoc creator on stunts and twists, using overwhelming strength to get blockers. As a run defender, he can stand his ground and be a consistent edge setter. But he is more of a build-up rusher than true bender, which limits his amounts of clean wins against offensive tackles.

Stats through Sept. 30: 14 tackles, 1.5 sacks, 2.5 tackles for loss, one interception for 27 yards and one touchdown

8. Charlie Becker, WR, Indiana*
Height: 6-4 | Weight: 208

Becker is primarily used as a vertical threat, and there are few college players who can match his straight-ahead speed. But he is more than just a threat with his legs; he's similar to an NBA rebounder with the way he wins 50-50 passes. That ability comes from a combination of elite body control at the catch point and A-plus hand-eye coordination, which helps him see the ball in slow motion. Becker does need to round out his route tree, showing NFL teams that he has more branches on it than just vertical patterns.

Stats through Sept. 30: 19 receptions for 370 receiving yards (19.5 per catch) and six touchdowns

9. Trevor Goosby, OT, Texas*
Height: 6-7 | Weight: 325

Goosby has a gangly build for a tackle prospect, which gives him excellent length to match and mirror defenders off the edge. His hand power and timing allow him to generate movement at the point of attack. But Goosby has lapses with his body balance and weight distribution, which can cause him to lean into blocks and slide off defenders. He is effective with adjusting to counter moves, which makes it difficult for rushers to unravel from him.

Stats through Sept. 30: 259 snaps, 0% pressure rate allowed, 3% blown run block rate

10. Jadan Baugh, RB, Florida*
Height: 6-1 | Weight: 225

Baugh is the top running back prospect in this class, a chiseled and powerful runner with timely short-area quickness. He activates his lower body to slither his way through creases, while also being able to simply plant his foot and accelerate through the line of scrimmage. Baugh doesn't have the home run speed to rattle off long touchdowns, but he has enough to generate explosive plays with the yardage that's available to him. He has a lot of work to do as a pass protector, showing inconsistency with his technique and in recognizing blitzing defenders.

Stats through Sept. 30: 83 carries for 600 yards (7.2 per carry) and 11 touchdowns; two receptions for 18 receiving yards

11. Drew Mestemaker, QB, Oklahoma State*
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 215

Mestemaker is my top quarterback prospect despite this being only his second season as a starter in high school and college. He has an unconventional style, holding the ball at his waistline before ripping a fiery, three-quarters release. Mestemaker has the confidence to test the tightest of windows from various platforms, but that can get the best of him and lead to turnovers. Plus, he can be oblivious to underneath defenders. Mestemaker is bit of a streaky passer, though his hot streaks feature plenty of "wow" moments. And he is capable of being a running threat.

Stats through Sept. 30: 95-of-141 passing (67.4% completion percentage) for 1,271 passing yards, 11 touchdowns and five interceptions; 13 carries for 106 rushing yards (8.2 per carry) and one touchdown

12. Cam Coleman, WR, Texas*
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 204

A lanky and long-striding target, Coleman is a no-nonsense route runner who quickly drives off the line of scrimmage when given free releases. He has routine hands and an extended catch radius that help him snatch the ball out of the air regardless of where it's located. And Coleman has an expansive route tree, which makes him a target at all three levels of the field. His biggest concern is getting past physical defenders at the line of scrimmage and at the top of his routes.

Stats through Sept. 30: 12 receptions for 208 receiving yards (17.3 per catch) and four touchdowns

13. Ashton Hampton, CB, Clemson*
Height: 6-2 | Weight: 205

Hampton is a physically imposing cornerback who strives to humiliate receivers at the line of scrimmage by getting his hands on them. Since most receivers struggle to untangle from his coverage, he would be ideal for press man coverage schemes at the next level. Hampton is also a forceful tackler on the perimeter, with lots of knockback strength when coming into contact with ball carriers. But he does need to be more disciplined with his timing in coverage.

Stats through Sept. 30: 10 tackles, one interception for 2 yards, seven passes defensed, 22.7% completion percentage allowed

14. Darian Mensah, QB, Miami*
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 205

Mensah is a locate-and-loft thrower who has a great sense of true progressions and can string together long stretches of accurate completions. He has great touch on passes, as he can drop throws right into the outstretched arms of targets. Mensah is also unafraid to throw into the teeth of blitzes and make defenses pay for trying to rush his throw plans. He is sufficient enough with his legs to buy time and make throws outside of structure. But Mensah has average velocity when forced to throw into tight windows. And he needs to improve his ball security, as rushers have had success jarring the ball loose from him in the pocket.

Stats through Sept. 30: 94-of-106 passing (88.7%) for 1,211 yards, 14 touchdown and zero interceptions; nine carries for 52 rushing yards (5.8 per carry) and one touchdown

15. Greg Johnson, G, Minnesota
Height: 6-6 | Weight: 325

Johnson is a hulking interior blocker whose strength helps him latch and sustain at the point of attack. He has a reliable anchor that helps him tether his feet and quickly stall pass-rush moves. In gap run schemes, Johnson has shown quickness when pulling. In zone run schemes, Johnson can be fluid enough to climb and cover up linebackers on the second level. A lot of Johnson's losses are a result of him relying solely on his upper body to generate torque and movement. His recovery athleticism is average, and he can face challenges when forced to readjust after being beaten quickly around either shoulder.

Stats through Sept. 30: 226 snaps, 0% pressure rate allowed, 0% blown run block rate

16. Trinidad Chambliss, QB, Ole Miss
Height: 6-0 | Weight: 205

A headache for the opposition in multiple ways, Chambliss can break down defenses with both his throwing ability and mobility. His excellent field vision complements a compact and fiery release, helping him anticipate and attack over the middle. Despite his lack of size, he can consistently reach all areas of the field. Chambliss also isn't afraid to welcome high-leverage moments, which he showed throughout last year's College Football Playoff and so far this season. His frame and age (he'll be 25 years old before next season) could inhibit his draft profile.

Stats through Sept. 30: 102-of-144 passing (70.8%) for 1,222 passing yards, eight touchdowns and three interceptions; 28 carries for 108 rushing yards (3.9 per carry) and four touchdowns

17. Arch Manning, QB, Texas*
Height: 6-4 | Weight: 222

Manning has prototypical size and a well-built frame for the position. His arm strength provides exciting plays when throwing to the intermediate and deep portions of the field, and his above-average mobility allows him to take off when defenses leave an opening. Manning is still only at best with concepts that allow him to execute simple reads. When trying to make full-field progressions, he can hold onto the ball too long. There are also too many moments when poor footwork and mechanics lead to scattershot ball placement.

Stats through Sept. 30: 73-of-115 passing (63.5%) for 862 passing yards, seven touchdowns and three interceptions; 32 carries for 82 rushing yards (2.6 per carry)

18. Chris Cole, LB, Georgia*
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 235

Cole is an easy moving, urgent defender from the second level. He has excellent lateral agility and pursuit speed to close on ball carriers in a hurry. But his ability to read and react to run concepts is still a work in progress, as his eyes can get fixated in the wrong spots. And he can be slow at recognizing concepts in zone coverage, leading to easy catches in his area. Cole is frequently used as a blitzer, which he does effectively.

Stats through Sept. 30: 18 tackles, 1.5 sacks, three tackles for loss, two fumble recoveries, one pass defensed

19. Ellis Robinson IV, CB, Georgia*
Height: 6-0 | Weight: 180

Robinson is an ultra-athletic cornerback whose quick feet and sudden change of direction helps him stay connected in man coverage. But there are times when Robinson gives up big gains because his technique tends to be abandoned. His best reps come in zone coverage, where he has a great feel for concepts unfolding. Robinson has excellent awareness with attacking the ball in flight, and he has a linebacker-like appetite for contact in run support.

Stats through Sept. 30: Eight tackles, three passes defensed, 63.6% completion percentage allowed

20. Dante Moore, QB, Oregon
Height: 6-3 | Weight: 220

From his footwork to throwing release, Moore is a natural in every area for the position. He orchestrates Oregon's up-tempo attack efficiently with B-level arm strength. His game is predicated upon rhythm, timing and anticipation, showing comfort with concepts to all levels of the field. Moore can routinely stack completions when protected. He isn't afraid to attack the seams and shred defenses. Moore is also an underrated runner, but he uses his mobility only as a last resort. He still needs to become more consistent against top-tier defenses and in withstanding early pressure. Moore has had stretches of bypassing open playmakers downfield to make safer throws underneath. There's still no timeline on when he will return for Oregon after sustaining a concussion against USC on Sept. 27.

Stats through Sept. 30: 69-of-99 passing (69.7%) for 926 passing yards, nine touchdowns and zero interceptions; 10 carries for minus-7 yards (minus-0.7 per carry)

21. Jamari Johnson, TE, Oregon
Height: 6-5 | Weight: 255

Johnson is a big playmaker in the passing game, especially over the middle of the field. He has natural hands and the catch radius to pluck balls outside his frame. As a route runner, Johnson wins with controlled tempos, decisiveness and spatial awareness. He can compete through contact when challenged, but he won't surprise defenders with his top-end speed or suddenness. Johnson also isn't a dynamic threat who can stack up extra yards after the catch that aren't created for him schematically. He isn't overly reliable on single blocks as a run blocker.

Stats through Sept. 30: 11 receptions for 176 receiving yards (16.0 per catch) and one touchdown

22. CJ Carr, QB, Notre Dame*
Height: 6-2 | Weight: 215

Carr is a refined pocket passer whose eyes, feet and throwing motion are always in cohesion. With an easy throwing motion, he is a decisive passer who trusts his eyes to pick apart defenses. He has a great feel for the types of passes that are needed, putting enough touch or velocity on them. And he is routinely in control at the line of scrimmage with protections and when calling audibles. Carr's overall arm strength and velocity are average. And he sometimes creates chaotic negative losses trying to make a positive play instead of moving on to the next play.

Stats through Sept. 30: 67-of-95 passing (70.5%) for 963 passing yards, nine touchdowns and one interception; eight carries for 13 yards (1.6 per carry) and two touchdowns

23. Trey'Dez Green, TE, LSU*
Height: 6-7 | Weight: 237

Green is like an NBA small forward on the turf, constantly presenting a tall task for defenses. As a true "F" tight end, he's a movable offensive weapon who provides most of value as a pass catcher from the slot or split out wide. Green can routinely glide past matchups with an expansive route tree through the middle of defenses. His ball tracking and leaping ability help him sky over defenders, especially in the red zone. Green's physicality as a blocker has improved, but his lack of bulk can be used against him inside of the box.

Stats through Sept. 30: 14 receptions for 222 receiving yards (15.9 per catch) and one touchdown

24. KJ Bolden, S, Georgia*
Height: 6-0 | Weight: 195

Bolden plays a variety of spots in Georgia's secondary but projects best as a center field free safety. He is a mistake eraser in the back end, showcasing range and instinctiveness to quickly bring a halt to plays. Bolden is an aggressive tackler who comes downhill with urgency. His lack of strength can hurt him in man coverage, as bigger receivers can outmuscle him and make catches through his frame.

Stats through Sept. 30: Eight tackles, one interception for 29 yards, one pass defensed, 50% completion percentage allowed

25. Trevor Lauck, OT, Iowa
Height: 6-5 | Weight: 314

Lauck is an old-school, tough offensive tackle. His playing style isn't flashy or glamorous; he simply collects wins in bunches by executing his hand power and physicality. Lauck has upper-tier upper-body strength and hands that are active when initiating contact. His pass sets are a bit unconventional given his average athleticism, but he's savvy with sorting and terminating rush moves. Lauck isn't firm on contact and can get moved off his spot, so he will need to learn to better churn his feet after the initiation process. He could improve his lower-body strength.

stories.headline: Jamal Shead, Raptors reach 3-year, $24M extension through 2029-30
stories.summary: Raptors guard Jamal Shead has agreed to a three-year, $24 million contract extension with the franchise, his agent, KJ Smith, told ESPN.
stories.body:
Toronto Raptors guard Jamal Shead has agreed to a three-year, $24 million contract extension with the franchise, his agent, KJ Smith, told ESPN on Thursday.

The new deal keeps Shead, 24, under contract through the 2029-30 season. He lands an extension just two seasons after the Houston product was selected with the 45th overall pick in the 2024 NBA draft.

The 6-foot-1 guard had 354 assists (5.4 per game) in 2025-26 -- a league-best off the bench and the most in franchise history for a reserve player. He played in all 82 regular-season games -- one of 18 NBA players to do so -- while averaging 6.6 points and 1.7 rebounds.

Shead saw action in seven playoff games (four starts), averaging nine points, five assists and 1.4 steals.

He ranked fifth in the league in assist-to-turnover ratio last season.

ESPN Research contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Lando Norris urges F1 and social media giants to help tackle abuse after Franco Colapinto ban feud
stories.summary: Lando Norris called on Formula 1 and social media companies to do more to combat online abuse after the torrent of messages he received following last weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Lando Norris called on Formula 1 and social media companies to do more to combat online abuse after the torrent of messages he received following last weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The comment sections of Norris' social media channels were filled with thousands of negative and hateful messages after he said in a postrace interview that Alpine driver Franco Colapinto should be banned for causing the collision that took his McLaren out of the race.

Two days after the event in Baku, Norris publicly apologized for his postrace comments in a message shared with his 11.9 million followers on Instagram.

Speaking ahead of this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Norris explained why he made the apology and called on the sport, social media channels and drivers to do more to prevent extreme comments, including death threats.

"I said what I wanted to Franco, and he's the only one really that I need to share my opinion with and share my apology with," Norris said. "I don't need to do it on social media, and I don't feel like I need to use social media to do such a thing, but at the same time, there obviously was a lot of that noise and stuff in the background, and I thought it was only sensible to announce or show that I made that apology.

"But yeah, at the same time, I do still see social media at times, and I saw some bits, some not so good, some better, but sadly that's what we deal with. I think a lot of sports deal with [it], some of it's down to just passion, and that's what you always have in sports.

"I think you see a lot more of it because social media is such an easy thing to share your opinions on. And to a certain extent, I completely respect it, but obviously to the extent of online abuse, death threats, all those things, those are things that I think are way too far beyond being a fan of a sport, or a driver, or a person, or an athlete, whatever it is.

"There's a line, but it's not new, it's something that's been around every sport for a long time, and I think just highlights more the fact that social media platforms, sports, need to do more, and maybe the people, the drivers, athletes, whoever, more to stop this kind of stuff from happening, because some people can deal with it much better than others."

Norris said the reaction he received on social media would not stop him from speaking his mind, even though he regretted his postrace comments in Baku.

"I should never have said the sort of stuff that I said, so I get why some people might have been more unhappy, let's just say upset, which is understandable," he added.

"Obviously there's that line which was crossed at times, quite a lot, which is not just being upset at someone, this is much, much worse.

"But I think I'm always happy, in general, in speaking my mind, and saying if I like things, don't like things, if I agree with things or not. I know I'm not able to please everyone, and you're never going to have everyone on your side, so I think that's normal enough, that's life, and that's what you have to come around to accept at the end of the day."

- Lewis Hamilton hits out at Ferrari hierarchy in Fred Vasseur defence: 'Point fingers somewhere else'

- Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia: Where were today's drivers when F1 last raced at Sepang?

- Max Verstappen steps in for GT race at Portimão amid two F1 triple-headers

Colapinto accepted Norris' apology earlier this week, but on Thursday said he was surprised the McLaren driver chose to be so public with his criticism after the race.

"I think he was in the heat of the moment ... He knows what comments create because he suffered from it," Colapinto said.

"He was probably the driver that was speaking the most about hate a couple of years ago, just a few seasons ago. So I was very surprised. But then, of course, he apologised.

"Unfortunately, he also got a lot of hate from it. But I also felt it's a tricky situation with the outside world. And that's why I think we need to be a bit safe inside about the things we say. And I understand it in the heat of the moment to say things like that."

Colapinto's fanbase has proved particularly vocal online and as recently as the Spanish Grand Prix last month turned on his Alpine teammate Pierre Gasly, with abuse that included messages sent to the Frenchman's family and girlfriend.

Asked what his message to those posting the negative comments online would be, Colapinto said: "My message is always the same, that they sometimes don't realise what you can create by writing in your keyword, and that we are humans, and it's not easy for us when we get these kind of things.

"I think it always goes to Argentinians, but we miss that it doesn't come only from Argentinians. It comes a lot from them, I fully agree. It doesn't just come from them, and they are extremely passionate, and they support me a lot. And it's bad, and they are bad many times, but it comes from all the world, and from many other fanbases.

"I don't know if we are not seeing it, I get loads of it and no one ever talks about it. I mean, it's fine because I don't look at social media too much. I don't go into it. But I know it affects a lot of people, and a lot of drivers, and a lot of families more than me.

"I hope that they improve. I've been asking for a long time. It's tricky for us drivers to control it. I think we are the ones to not do them more. But we are also really striving to improve the situation by ourselves. Because we try -- for me, it's been since last year that I've been talking about it. I am doing my best, but it's tricky."

In 2023 F1's governing body, the FIA, set up the United Against Online Abuse (UAOA) commission, which as recently as this year's British Grand Prix received the collective support of all 22 drivers in F1.

On its website, the UAOA says it "aims to design, develop and implement practical actions that can protect the integrity of sports across the world as safe and inclusive spaces for competitors, officials, journalists, and fans alike."

stories.headline: After a shocking offseason, the Flyers fight regression
stories.summary: Philly was one of the NHL's biggest surprise teams last season -- and now has to back up the bold moves of its GM.
stories.body:
VOORHEES, N.J. -- The Philadelphia Flyers were one of the NHL's genuine surprises last season, making the playoffs for the first time since 2020 and advancing to the second round with a series win over the rival Pittsburgh Penguins.

General manager Danny Briere had overseen their rebuild since 2023. "Brick by brick," he said, sitting in his office at the team's practice facility. "Not trying to get ahead of ourselves. Trying to do it right."

But this offseason the Flyers put the meticulous bricklaying on hold and attempted to just buy someone else's furnished mansion. They signed Anaheim Ducks center Leo Carlsson, 21, to a five-year, $90 million offer sheet in a move that changed the financial landscape of player salaries and nearly shifted the competitive balance in the NHL with it.

The moment it was announced, Briere started hearing from his peers.

"The one that kept coming back the most was, 'You do what's right for your team.' We all have different things to deal with. There's nothing wrong with what you did. You played by the rules and it's there for anybody to use," he said.

New Jersey Devils GM Sunny Mehta always thought it was possible that a team would back up the truck for a restricted free agent the way the Flyers did.

"The only thing that you just aren't sure about is the taboo of the offer sheet. Will people actually do this?" he said. "You hear people talk about this every year. Doing it is a whole separate story. And someone actually did it."

Philadelphia center Trevor Zegras knew Carlsson from their days together in Anaheim and was excited by Briere's bold move -- even if the Flyers group chat was eerily quiet. "Maybe guys were just hoping that it would end up going through. Maybe they didn't want to jinx it," Zegras said.

Whether it was jinxed or not, the Ducks matched the offer sheet, depriving the Flyers of a potential franchise center. But Briere's move changed things. Carlsson's $18 million annual cap hit, the highest in the NHL this season, reset the bar for other's contracts. That included one the Ducks had to give their leading goal scorer Cutter Gauthier, who eventually signed for six years at a $13.5 million annual cap hit.

Gauthier was drafted by the Flyers at No. 5 in 2022 but was traded to Anaheim after telling Briere he didn't want to play for Philadelphia. One theory that emerged in the wake of the Carlsson offer sheet -- shared with ESPN by a player agent -- was that Flyers ownership greenlit the contract as the ultimate long-term vengeance with Anaheim after the Gauthier saga.

"They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us,'" the agent said.

Briere denied that the Flyers had targeted the Ducks.

"My job's a lot more important than trying to get back at people. Look, we're all competitive. We're all trying to win. That scenario was what we felt was the right one for us," he said. "It wasn't my goal to put Anaheim in that position or [Ducks GM] Pat Verbeek in that position. We had a great relationship with them. We just felt we had a chance to improve our team, not give up any of our roster players. It just made sense for us at that moment. It was nothing more than that."

The offer sheet's ancillary benefit was as an endorsement of the Flyers' progress.

"It was cool. Any time your general manager tries to do something to better the team, it feels good. Love the direction that we're headed," Zegras said.

"I hope they're rejuvenated by it, even though it didn't work," Briere said. "We believe in our team. They took a big step last year and we wanted to show them that it didn't go unnoticed."

But the general manager also hopes his young team doesn't get tripped up during that leap forward.

THEIR FIRST STEP into this season was an embarrassing stumble for the Flyers. The Penguins walked out of Philadelphia having drubbed their hosts 7-0 on Wednesday night, the largest margin of defeat in a season opener in Flyers' history.

"I honestly don't have an answer. I don't think we won a battle tonight. They did everything better than us," Tocchet said. "There are alarming things out there. I don't know if guys are reading their press clippings, but it wasn't good."

The word regression is used a lot in the NHL, whether it's a player trying to sustain a high shooting percentage or a team trying to build on an unexpected playoff berth. There are all sorts of reasons the Flyers could drop from their 98-point total from last season -- injuries, bad puck luck, a downtick in their goaltending performance -- but the one Briere is watching closely is overconfidence.

"The part that keeps me up at night is having some of your players feel complacent, feel like they've made it," he said. "I'm worried that coming back, they'll think it's a little easier than they realize. If that happens, we could have a setback."

He has used winger Matvei Michkov as a cautionary tale. He scored 26 goals in 80 games as a rookie before having what the team felt was an underwhelming follow-up, which included a callout about his conditioning from new coach Rick Tocchet. Briere said he hoped young forwards such as Denver Barkey and Calder Trophy candidate Porter Martone didn't fall into the same trap.

"We talk to them. We address it with them and that's all part of our development team to getting them ready, using examples and trying to prepare them for what to expect this year," he said.

Michkov, for his part, showed up to camp in great shape and with "pep in his step," according to Briere. "I think we saw him mature as the season went on last year. Everybody has a different path. You all wish that guys were like Sidney Crosby and were a total pro at 16 years old, but the reality is those [players] are really rare," he said.

Another player on a different path last season was Zegras, the 25-year-old center they acquired from Anaheim in June 2025. Both Briere and Tocchet challenged him to level up his game with the Flyers, and Zegras reignited his star in the NHL: Scoring 26 goals and 41 assists in 81 games, and earning a four-year, $36.5 million contract extension.

Briere isn't concerned about Zegras falling into old habits now that he has signed an extension.

"We've had many talks about facing the pressure, playing in big games, not afraid of big moments. I was really, really impressed with how he handled it, how he played hard, because that was a little bit of a knock on him early in his career," Briere said. "I think he's matured a lot, took a big step forward last year. He started understanding better. He never played in a playoff game before, and that experience was huge for him."

To that end, the worst thing that happened to the Flyers last season might end up being the best thing for them: getting mauled by the Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes in a second-round sweep.

"They were good. They were experienced. They knew how to handle it and they did a better job," Briere said. "But that experience for us was I think amazing."

That also goes for the Flyers' journey to a playoff berth, winning huge games down the stretch, and their first-round win over the Penguins, in which Philadelphia jumped out to a 3-0 series lead before holding off Pittsburgh's rally to win in six games.

"Last year was such a different experience," Flyers winger Travis Konecny said. "Coming back, we're still talking about it. So that tells me guys have had it in the back of their head all summer. They're hungry. They want more."

Briere won't make any grand proclamations about the Flyers this season.

"You're not going to like my answer. I know it's boring. But we're still a young team," he said. "We expect it to be harder. For me, it's exciting, because we're at a time now where you want to see how your guys handle the hard. We're not going to creep up on anyone this year."

Briere hoped Carlsson might be part of that group for the Flyers, but he's wearing a different shade of orange and black this season. If the opportunity presents itself again, Briere said he won't hesitate to aggressively augment an already promising roster.

"We were a bad team for way too long to just throw away the cap space that we've built and the freedom that we're able to have. We're not going to be reckless about it," he said. "If something comes up that makes sense, we won't be afraid to take a swing again."

stories.headline: Banned and crowned: Isaac Heeney wins Swans' best and fairest
stories.summary: Isaac Heeney has been named Sydney's best and fairest, but he and fellow Sydney stars were notable absentees from the club's end-of-season awards night.
stories.body:
An absent Isaac Heeney has been crowned Sydney's best and fairest as the spectre of sexual assault allegations continues to loom over the AFL club.

Heeney was not at Sydney Town Hall to accept his third consecutive Bob Skilton medal, having requested to skip the club's Thursday awards night.

Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were also absent after serving a club-imposed suspension with Heeney throughout the finals.

Despite missing Round 24 and two finals -- which also counted for award calculations -- Heeney polled 431 votes to comfortably claim the club's highest individual annual honour ahead of ruck Brodie Grundy (400) and key forward Charlie Curnow (398).

Four of the suspended Swans finished in the top 10 of the count, with Warner placing fourth ahead of Blakey (seventh) and Jordon (10th).

The club had opted against changing eligibility and voting criteria for the Bob Skilton medal, following suit after the AFL did the same with the Brownlow Medal.

The league did not invite Heeney or Warner to last week's Brownlow ceremony.

In his awards ceremony speech, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham said the reasoning behind the club's eligibility criteria was two-fold - protecting the integrity of votes; and ensuring off-field matters were separate from on-field performance.

"We do not believe it would have been appropriate to retrospectively remove votes that have already been cast owing to the subsequent incident," Pridham said.

"The medals awarded tonight acknowledge on-field performance across the season.

"Erasing a season of football after the fact would, in our opinion, be inappropriate and in excess of a sanction.

"I can assure you that we did not make any decisions we have made in recent times like that.

"I respect that some people in this room and beyond may not agree with where we have landed tonight.

"It has been very, very difficult, but let me be equally clear that these decisions to allow the players to remain eligible does not diminish our concern and respect for everyone involved in this."

Independent of the AFL-endorsed club bans for what the Swans termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards", a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel is ongoing.

Detectives in early September travelled to NSW to interview a 30-year-old Maroubra man, a 25-year-old Paddington man and two Randwick men aged 25 and 26.

It is understood the men interviewed were Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Blakey.

No charges have been laid. AAP is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

The five banned players have since returned to Swans headquarters after serving their suspension and individually offered apologies to colleagues and teammates following their team's preliminary final loss to Fremantle.

Heeney was the only player after the club meeting to address media and did so with a brief statement.

"It was really nice to address the whole club," the 30-year-old said on September 23.

"Extremely thankful they could give us their time and understanding, so yeah, it was really good."

Victoria Police's eight-week timeline prediction - which was first flagged on September 2 - on their investigation into the Pullman Hotel incident takes in the free agency and trade period (October 2-14).

All five players are contracted for next year, with Blakey signed to the club until 2031.

Warner and Jordon come off contract at the end of 2027, while Heeney and Bice are signed until the end of 2028.

Multiple reports have suggested Blakey is seeking a trade to a Victorian club, but Sydney football boss Leon Cameron dismissed those rumblings as "speculation" in September.

stories.headline: St. Louis up to 2nd place with unbeaten run now at 17 games
stories.summary: Simon Becher and Tomas Ostrak each scored late in the second half as St. Louis City SC beat the New York Red Bulls 3-0 on Wednesday night.
stories.body:
Simon Becher and Tomas Ostrak each scored late in the second half as St. Louis City SC beat the New York Red Bulls 3-0 on Wednesday night.

St. Louis (13-6-8) extended its unbeaten streak to 17 matches in MLS play and moved up to second place in MLS' Western Conference table.

New York (9-12-6) entered having conceded just two goals in its last four games, with Ethan Horvath recording three shutouts.

The Red Bulls had won their last two games, but were without rising stars Adri Mehmeti and Julian Hall for the game, with the pair away on national team duty for the United States.

Rafael Navarro opened the scoring just five minutes into the game when he redirected Conrad Wallem's header across the goal.

Becher capitalized on a New York turnover deep in its own half to make it 2-0 in the 87th minute. Ostrak sent in a rebound in stoppage time.

Roman Bürki made four saves to earn his third clean sheet of the season for St. Louis.

It was the first time New York and St. Louis have met during the regular season.

St. Louis hosts the LA Galaxy next on Oct. 11, while the Red Bulls play San Diego FC at home the day before.

Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

stories.headline: Ivan: Nathan Cleary can get even better after Dally M
stories.summary: Ivan Cleary has spoken of the horror of watching his son Nathan's leg injury, and a belief he can still get better again after winning his first Dally M.
stories.body:
Ivan Cleary has admitted watching his son Nathan suffer a badly broken leg marked one of the hardest days of his career, feeling the line between father and coach blurred for the first time.

But the veteran Penrith mentor is insistent his son Nathan still has more levels to attain once he returns from his injury, following his landmark Dally M victory on Wednesday night.

Cleary's Dally M triumph completed the Penrith halfback's rugby league box set, having now claimed every major team and individual honour available to him by age 28.

Unable to attend in person after being released from hospital following emergency surgery on his leg, the Panthers halfback collected the game's top honour while in a wheelchair at home.

Coach Ivan also appeared emotional during Nathan's pre-recorded speech, after the trophy was hand-delivered to the halfback earlier in the day.

"His voice perked up from what it's been the past couple of days," Ivan told AAP.

"It's a pretty amazing award. You don't play the game for individual awards, but it's certainly nice to be recognised.

"Particularly this award, it's pretty much the No.1 award in the game."

Reminded that his son had now scaled virtually every possible mountain in the sport, the Penrith coach insisted there were still improvements left in his son's game.

"It's crazy," Ivan said.

"I know he'd say it and I probably think a bit the same. You don't reflect too much when it's still going on. But when you put it like that, it's amazing.

"But I know there is so much more to come as well, and I know he thinks that way as well."

Nathan has received positive early news from surgeons after the operation on his compound fracture and dislocated ankle, as a result of a hip-drop tackle in Sunday's preliminary-final loss to Newcastle.

He will soon undergo surgery on other foot after fighting through a broken bone to play the Knights, but Penrith are hopeful he will be right for round one in 2027.

"Sunday was definitely one of the harder days I have been through," coach Cleary said.

"It's the first time where the line of dad and coach got a bit blurred. And the loss, I guess we have had a lot of good days so you can't have it all your way.

"Very emotional, but life goes on."

Footage has also emerged of fullback Dylan Edwards not only being horrified by the graphic injury at first, but then also trying to stop Nathan from seeing it.

"I was just trying to keep him calm as I could," Edwards said.

"To his credit he is a tough person. And the way he was handling that was incredible.

"It was gut-wrenching, something you're not used to seeing on the footy field."

Edwards, meanwhile, is still hopeful of being able to represent Australia at the World Cup after avoiding knee surgery following a PCL injury in the loss.

"I'm not sure, I have to talk to Kevvie (coach Kevin Walters)," Edwards said, while wearing a brace at the Dally Ms.

stories.headline: Inside Fever guard Caitlin Clark's new Nike signature shoe
stories.summary: Caitlin Clark's signature shoe and clothing line lands Thursday. The Fever guard and a Nike designer shared details with ESPN.
stories.body:
CAITLIN CLARK CASUALLY leans against a wall minutes before shootaround the morning her Indiana Fever open their WNBA playoff series against the Las Vegas Aces. A half-smirk spreads across her face, an expression that often appears when she talks. The look isn't even intentional, despite being the sort of glance one gives when there's an inside joke no one else knows.

That same tight-lipped, dimple-inducing grin is plastered on the side of a building across the street from Gainbridge Fieldhouse, the Fever's home in Indianapolis.

Accompanying the knowing glance is the phrase: Nothing special to see here*. The asterisk is no typo.

Clark's debut signature shoe from Nike -- the Caitlin 1 -- officially goes on sale Thursday, and the rollout has already begun. The "Caitlin Blue" and yellow "Warning Code" colorways are up first. As the release date approached, Nike began to flood all platforms with an ad campaign promoting the first signature shoe of one of the most well-known athletes on the planet.

"It speaks very much to who I am, like this ordinary person that at times does some super extraordinary things on the court," Clark told ESPN in an exclusive interview. "But to me, that's just what I do.

"I understand, to other people, it's incredible and they could never comprehend doing those things. But at the same time, I feel like I do everything that they do, whether that's play golf or eat cereal for breakfast or whatever it is."

The campaign, designed in Clark's image, is a sneaky mix of bravado and normalcy. A blend of you-can't-be-me and I'm-you-too.

Along Pennsylvania Street, across from the Fever arena, the picture is a selfie from Clark while lying on a couch. But that's just one billboard. A television spot features the 2024 No. 1 draft pick and Rookie of the Year sitting at a kitchen table eating cereal -- LogO's featuring bite-sized morsels shaped like her logo and the No. 2, of course. Another version shows Clark packing a luggage bag full of Caitlin 1s in a variety of colors before heading off frame. She doesn't say a single world in either, but Nick Offerman does the talking.

In an ad looking to play off the dichotomy of Clark's girl-next-door-off-the-court-but-devastating-basketball-world-destroyer-on-the-court persona, having the actor known for his deadpan portrayal of Ron Swanson on "Parks and Recreation" deadpanning the voiceover is a purposeful choice.

"It's like the irony of everything," Clark explained. "I hope that's what people are getting. The boring part of it is like it's trying to be ironic. And it's not boring. It's just an every-day-in-the-office [thing]. And that's what so extraordinary about it. I loved it."

THE NIKE STAFF headquartered eight miles outside of Portland, Oregon, racked up frequent flyer miles over the last two years. Trips to Indiana became a regularity as members of the design group would travel to meet Clark, just to get to know her. The whole concept of the shoe and subsequent marketing campaign are deeply personal. Before they could dive into the details, they needed to learn about the young superstar's world. They attended workouts and practices. Spent time at her home. That's where she seemed most comfortable and creative.

A level of trust also had to be built as Clark can be demanding, and that's putting it lightly. Just ask an official, whether she's actually playing in the game or not. Coaches and teammates have even gotten a taste. The design team at Nike quickly found out.

"She has these extended and elevated expectations out the gate," Nike footwear designer Ben Nethongkome said, "whereas other athletes in the past may have just been super happy to be part of the Nike family and just kind of go with the flow. Hers [is] like, 'I need this. There's a lot of anticipation around my product. This needs to be a banger out the gate.'

"So that added pressure. We knew that was gonna be there prior to coming in, but it only juiced up the team even more for us to create better work."

Creating signature designs can be an arduous process. There has to be a blend of function and individuality. Nike cranks out plenty of models that are specifically constructed for excellence on the court. Signatures must have a connection to the individual player and meet their desires. Some emphasize a look that works both on the court and in the streets. Different styles of players need different construction to fit their games.

And Clark wanted the best of both worlds as she joins A'ja Wilson (Nike), Angel Reese (Reebok), Breanna Stewart (Puma), Sabrina Ionescu (Nike) and Jacy Sheldon (HOLO) as active WNBA players with a signature sneaker.

For example, the 6-foot point guard who finished the 2026 regular season ranked No. 2 in points and assists per game insisted on function surrounding one thing: speed. She wanted help to stop on a dime, help to step back quicker and help to shoot faster. Those are the key parts of Clark's game, and any shoe had to amplify those.

So the traction had to be elite. An early pattern had to be ditched because it leaned a bit too heavy on aesthetic as opposed to function. They settled on a "multidirectional fanning traction pattern" that maximized the ability to change directions. A "responsive Nike Air turbo zoom unit" curves to the foot to assist the ability to create space on those side-steps and step-backs that are a staple of her game. The "Nike Opticast" upper portion of the shoe features arc-like waves meant to represent her shot chart and ever-expanding shooting range. But it's functional, Nethongkome explained, like fingers to wrap and support the forefront of the foot.

"That's what makes a signature model a signature model," said Nethongkome, who worked on the Ionescu and Wilson lines. "What makes [the] signature is these touches, these sprinkles of the athlete DNA, the thumbprint on the shoe. We've had times where the product tested really well, but it didn't meet the expectations of Caitlin Clark from a visual perspective. So, we had to go back to the drawing board and make some design tweaks to bring back that balance of, [it] can't all be science."

Alex Zerzan, Nike product line manager, added, "What you're seeing is that perfect blend of when art and science comes to life."

The art part is what everyone sees. Nodules of "22" and "CC" across the upperway. Swooshes that play on her initials and the 3-point arc. A seemingly endless array of colorways. In Game 1 of the opening round against the Las Vegas Aces, Clark debuted the "Berry Fade" edition that features a gradient fading from a popping red to purple on the left sneaker to the opposite fading on the right. After seeing the original design, it was Clark who requested the mirror flip from the left and right shoe. One colorway is inspired by Taylor Swift, with friendship bracelet beads on the laces. Kansas City Chiefs coach Andy Reid posted a video of him with his Chiefs-inspired pair nicknamed "Sea of Red."

"No decision on this shoe was made without Caitlin being involved," Zerzan said.

PEOPLE STILL TALK about Spike Lee's Mars Blackmon character who starred in the ad campaign for Michael Jordan's signature shoe. More recently, Wilson's A'One debuted last year with a campaign that featured a young Black girl's life, using the song from the hand game "Miss Mary Mack" and an iteration directed by Malia Obama. These are the messaging opportunities that can last a lifetime.

So while the design of the shoe is one thing, the marketing campaign is another. Clark wanted to give insight into who she is as a person and even studied past campaigns during the process. Everything revolves around the tongue-in-cheek tagline: Nothing special to see here*.

"There's an asterisk, like, this is special," Clark said. "I view myself as an entertainer and you're coming to watch the show. ... This is special what we're doing.

"At the same time, I like to think when I step off the court, I have regular hobbies like all of you. I garden. I play golf. I sit and watch TV, this and that. ... So, it's like, yeah, nothing special to see here wink-wink. But then at the same time, I do all these other things that are normal like everybody else."

One thing that isn't normal is waiting on a special gift from Ron Swanson, err, Nick Offerman. Who knew the actor who played Swanson had some of the character's skill set in real life? Swanson was an anti-government, live-off-the-land master woodworker. Offerman at least has that last part, and he received an endorsement for the gig from "Ted Lasso" actor Jason Sudeikis, who has a close friendship with Clark.

So there's a one-of-a-kind shoe case in the works straight from a Primetime Emmy Award-winning actor for the one-of-a-kind player.

Nothing special to see here.

"I just love his voice and the tone he has, and it's been super cool to see all of that come to life," Clark said. "His tone and the way he comes across is perfect for what we want to convey to everybody."

stories.headline: Which Premier League players got injured in the international break?
stories.summary: All the latest news and updates on Premier League stars injuries during the first international break of the 2026-2027 club season
stories.body:
Premier League teams will be watching and hoping their star players remain healthy throughout the international break.

However, some have already sustained injuries while playing for their countries. Premier League matches resume on Oct. 10.

ESPN will be tracking the latest injuries and updates for your club's players:

Kai Havertz (Arsenal)

Arsenal's Kai Havertz was forced off in the 30th minute of the game between Netherlands and Germany on September 24th with what was described as a muscle injury.

"Both are currently undergoing an MRI," Jurgen Klopp said on RTL about Havertz and Jamal Musiala. "I hope we get the diagnosis [on Thursday] evening. But of course, this isn't great. I hope it's nothing serious. The lads are probably out for us. But hopefully, they'll be back in action relatively quickly."

On September 25 the German Football Association confirmed the attacker would be leaving Klopp's camp and return to Arsenal after suffering what they describe as a 'muscle strain.'

Brian Brobbey (Sunderland)

The powerful Sunderland attacker was also injured in the same game after picking up what looked like a hamstring injury while running for the ball. He immediately went down and signalled to the sideline.

He left the field of his own accord but did have a heavy limp as he walked down the tunnel.

Netherlands boss Xavi Hernandez said after the game: "Brian is indeed injured."

Brobbey was replaced by Joshua Zirkzee in the Dutch squad.

Zion Suzuki (Aston Villa)

The goalkeeper linked up with the Japan squad but according to reports missed the main group training session on September 22nd, according to local reports. Instead he was put on an individual session for a rib injury.

Suzuki was subsequently left out of Japan's matchday squad entirely for Thursday's 3-1 victory over Uruguay.

Dan Ballard (Sunderland)

The Sunderland defender suffered a reported hamstring injury during Northern Ireland's 1-0 victory over Georgia in the UEFA Nations League.

With the score still 0-0 as the match moved into stoppage time, Ballard chased back as Georgia counter-attacked and pulled up clutching the back of his thigh, unable to finish the match in Tbilisi.

Speaking immediately after Friday's match, manager Michael O'Neill said it was too soon to know the extent of his latest injury but will definitely miss the next three Northern Ireland games.

"We'll scan him tomorrow (Saturday), but he's certainly not going to be available for the next three games."

Alexander Isak (Liverpool)

Alexander Isak is returning to Liverpool after sustaining a "minor injury" on international duty.

The striker scored and played the full 90 minutes in Sweden's 2-1 victory over Romania in the Nations League on Friday.

But Isak, who has made a strong start to the season for Liverpool, will not feature in matches against Poland, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Romania over the remainder of the extended international break.

Bruno Fernandes (Manchester United)

The Manchester United midfielder was left out of Portugal's squad for Sunday's game against Norway.

"He played with an injury he brought from Manchester United," Portugal boss Jorge Jesus said. "He really wanted to play against Wales."

Patrick Dorgu (Manchester United)

The news for Manchester United fans who saw Fernandes absent worsened on Sunday when Dorgu was injured.

The left wing-back limped out of Denmark's match against Wales after 30 minutes.

Denmark head coach Brian Riemer told broadcaster TV2 after the game: "He has an injury and has to go home."

Cody Gakpo (Liverpool)

Liverpool forward Gakpo lasted only 17 minutes of the Netherlands' match against Serbia on Sunday. It means Liverpool are sweating over the fitness of Isak and Gakpo.

He looked in pain as he held the lower part of his right leg.

"It's his ankle, that's all I know," Netherlands boss Xavi Hernández said. "Tomorrow we will know, but hopefully it's not too important."

Noussair Mazraoui (Manchester United)

The United full-back was forced out of Morocco's Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Lesotho after 69 minutes. He was holding his back while on the floor after a challenge.

Nico O'Reilly (Manchester City)

O'Reilly missed England's win against Czechia on Tuesday night after also missing training on Monday. Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha was called into the matchday squad. O'Reilly returned to Manchester for further treatment before England played Croatia.

Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham Hotspur)

The Tottenham defender Jan Paul van Hecke picked up a foot injury in the Netherlands' clash with Serbia and withdrew from the Netherlands' squad during a training session.

No replacement will be called up for van Hecke. He is now returning to Spurs.

International breaks this season

1. Sept. 21-Oct. 6 (between Premier League gameweeks 5 and 6)

2. Nov. 9-Nov. 17 (between Premier League gameweeks 10 and 11)

3. March 22-March 30 (between Premier League gameweeks 30 and 31)
